explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent due to two fundamental differences: the join type and the join condition. Q1 performs a `LEFT OUTER JOIN` on the condition `INSTRUCTOR.ID > TEACHES.ID`, which includes all instructors regardless of a match and pairs them with teaching records having a smaller ID. Q2 performs an `INNER JOIN` (using implicit comma-join syntax) on `INSTRUCTOR.ID = TEACHES.ID`, which only includes instructors who have a teaching record with the exact same ID. This means Q1 can produce NULLs for non-matching instructors and uses a non-equi join, while Q2 only returns exact matches and will never produce NULLs for the joined columns.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample includes two instructors with IDs 10 and 20, and two teaching records with IDs 10 and 15. In Q1, instructor 10 finds no match for `ID > TEACHES.ID` and thus appears with a NULL `COURSE_ID` due to the LEFT JOIN. Instructor 20 matches both teaching records. In Q2, only instructor 10 finds an exact ID match. This results in completely different outputs.

q1: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>4) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
q2: WITH S AS (SELECT ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR FROM TAKES NATURAL JOIN SECTION GROUP BY ID, TIME_SLOT_ID, YEAR HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID)>5) SELECT DISTINCT ID,NAME FROM S NATURAL JOIN STUDENT
explanation: The two queries are designed to find students based on the number of distinct time slots they have taken courses in during a single year. Q1 selects students who have taken courses in more than 4 distinct time slots (`HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 4`). Q2 is stricter, requiring more than 5 distinct time slots (`HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT TIME_SLOT_ID) > 5`). The point of divergence is a student who has taken courses in exactly 5 distinct time slots in a year. This student's count of 5 satisfies the condition of Q1 (5 > 4) but not Q2 (5 > 5), causing Q1 to return the student while Q2 returns an empty set.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample contains one student (ID 101) who, in the year 2023, takes five different sections. Each of these sections is assigned a unique time slot ID (from 1 to 5). When the queries are run, the aggregation for student 101 in year 2023 yields a count of 5 distinct time slots. This count meets Q1's criteria (`> 4`) but fails Q2's (`> 5`), thus producing different results.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE WHERE CREDITS=(SELECT MAX(CREDITS) FROM COURSE)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT DEPT_NAME FROM COURSE AS C JOIN (SELECT MAX(CREDITS) AS MAX_CREDITS FROM COURSE GROUP BY DEPT_NAME) AS A WHERE C.CREDITS = A.MAX_CREDITS
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because they compare course credits against different maximums. Q1 calculates a single, global maximum credit value across all courses and finds departments offering courses with that specific value. In contrast, Q2 calculates the maximum credit value for each department individually, creating a set of local maximums. It then uses a CROSS JOIN to find any department that offers a course whose credit value matches any of these local maximums. Consequently, Q2 can include departments whose courses do not have the global maximum credit value, but match the maximum of another department.
counterexample_dsp: The counterexample contains two departments, CS (ID 10) and EE (ID 20). The highest credit course overall is in CS with 4 credits. The EE department's highest credit course is 3 credits. The CS department also offers a 3-credit course. Q1 will only return CS (10), as it's the only department with the global max of 4 credits. Q2 will return both CS (10) and EE (20) because the set of per-department maximums is {4, 3}, and both departments offer courses with credits of either 3 or 4.
